guidebook.intro: Greetings are the heart of conversation in Busoga. Nobody asks for directions or buys a mango before saying hello first.

tips.title: Greetings follow the clock
body: Until about midday, ask **Wasuuze otya?**, literally “how did you sleep?”. Answer **Nsuuze bulungi** (I slept well) or just **Bulungi**.
Later in the day, switch to **Osiibye otya?**, “how have you spent the day?”. **Oli otya?** works at any time.

tips.title: One person or many
body: Greetings change when you talk to a group. The singular forms in this unit start with **w-** or **o-**; the plural forms start with **mw-** or **mu-**.

tips.title: Long vowels, single consonants
body: A doubled vowel (**aa**, **ee**, **ii**) is held a little longer, and length changes meaning, so say **Weebale** with a long **ee**. Unlike Luganda, Lusoga rarely doubles consonants: Luganda **kkumi**, **ssente** and **ggwe** are **ikumi**, **sente** and **iwe** in Lusoga.
Lusoga is written as it sounds: every letter is pronounced, and vowels sound much like Spanish or Italian vowels.

culture.title: Take time to greet
body: A greeting is a short conversation, not a single word. People ask after your health, your night and your work before getting to business. Rushing it can seem rude.

culture.title: Sebo and nyabo
body: Add **sebo** (sir) or **nyabo** (madam) to be polite with anyone older than you or anyone you don’t know. In traditional settings, people may kneel to greet elders as a sign of respect.

culture.title: Gyebale ko
body: Say **Gyebale ko** to anyone who is working: a shopkeeper, a farmer, a friend cooking. The usual reply is **Weebale** or **Kale**.
